question: Let \( S \) be the set of sides and diagonals of a regular pentagon. A pair of elements of \( S \) are selected at random without replacement. What is the probability that the two chosen segments have the same length?
solution:
The pentagon has five sides and five diagonals. To count the diagonals, each of the five vertices connects to two nonadjacent vertices, counting each diagonal twice, so there are \(5\cdot2/2=5\).

Rotating the regular pentagon through \(72^\circ\) carries sides to sides and diagonals to diagonals, so all sides have one common length and all diagonals have one common length. These lengths differ: otherwise three consecutive vertices would form an equilateral triangle, whose angle at the middle vertex would be \(60^\circ\), whereas the pentagon's interior angle is
\[
\frac{(5-2)180^\circ}{5}=108^\circ.
\]
Whatever segment is chosen first, exactly four other segments have its length. Without replacement, nine segments remain, all equally likely as the second choice. Thus every possible first choice gives the same matching probability,
\[
\boxed{\frac49},
\]
which is choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).
